name: Wave
tagline: Free accounting and invoicing software for small businesses.
description: Wave is free accounting and invoicing for small businesses: unlimited invoices with a Pay Now button, expense tracking, and bank reconciliation.
pros: The core is recorded as genuinely free — invoicing, expense tracking, and bank reconciliation at no cost, with unlimited invoicing named in this repository's freelancer ranking
Invoices end in a prominent Pay Now button linking to Stripe or PayPal, so payment is requested from the document itself

content.title: What Wave carries at no cost
content.body: Wave is filed here as free accounting and invoicing software for small businesses, and this repository's accounting ranking describes it as a genuinely free platform covering invoicing, expense tracking, and bank reconciliation at the entry level. The pricing guide places that model beside other freemium products: basic accounting features at no cost, with revenue drawn from payment processing fees and premium add-ons instead of a subscription. The description on this page comes from records the repository already holds — rankings, guides, comparison pages, and the fields stored alongside this review — rather than from anyone having opened a Wave account.

content.title: Invoices with a Pay Now button
content.body: Wave's invoicing surface is described in this repository's freelancer hub in practical terms: an invoice carries line items, rates, and payment terms, and ends with a prominent Pay Now button linking to Stripe or PayPal. That button is the piece connecting billing to cash, since the customer pays from the invoice rather than after a reminder, and it is also where the product's revenue model enters the transaction. The same hub groups Wave with FreshBooks and HoneyBook as the quick route to a professional invoice, while the freelancer ranking adds unlimited invoicing on the free option. The recorded invoice features are:
items: Line items, rates, and payment terms laid out on the invoice
A prominent Pay Now button linking to Stripe or PayPal
Unlimited invoicing recorded on Wave's free option
A path from time entry to a paid invoice for service businesses
Expense tracking and bank reconciliation sitting beside the billing

content.title: Bank reconciliation as the recorded core
content.body: Bank reconciliation sits in the same recorded trio as invoicing and expense tracking, which is what makes Wave a set of books rather than an invoice generator. This repository's accounting-selection guide lists reconciliation among the month-end steps a business should document before buying software, and the accounting ranking names it as one of the three things the free Wave covers. The shape implied by those records is a bank feed matched against recorded income and expenses, with the reconciled result feeding whatever statements the business needs. Nothing in the dataset describes inventory, project profitability, or multi-entity consolidation for Wave, which lines up with the guide that places it at the entry level for sole proprietors with simple finances.

content.title: How a free product earns revenue
content.body: This page records Wave's pricing model as free, with a price range of Free, and the repository's pricing guide explains how products of this shape pay for themselves: basic accounting features at no cost, generating revenue through payment processing fees and premium add-ons. The accounting ranking records the fee side more specifically, attaching a percentage-plus-fixed charge to credit card transactions and a percentage charge to bank payments, so cost rises with money collected rather than with seats. A business sending a handful of invoices therefore runs the tool for nothing, while a business in heavy payment volume funds the account through transactions. The free record and the add-on record are not in conflict: the core is free, and the paid part attaches to payments.

content.title: The ceiling our guides put on Wave
content.body: The clearest limit in this repository is written into a guide rather than a plan table: the QuickBooks-versus-Xero article tells readers to consider Wave for very basic accounting when a business is sending under five invoices and ten transactions a month. That sentence is the closest thing on file to a documented capacity boundary for the product, and it sits alongside the accounting-selection guide, which groups Wave with ZipBooks as free or very low-cost accounting for sole proprietors and freelancers with simple finances. Beyond volume, our records do not describe inventory, project profitability, or consolidation for Wave — gaps in what the dataset holds, rather than statements that the product lacks those things.

content.title: Where small teams start with Wave
content.body: Six ranking pages in this repository repeat the same position: small teams typically start with Wave, which carries the most accessible entry point in those rankings. The line appears across the budgeting, expense management, free accounting, expense tracking, cloud ERP, and ERP lists, which makes it a consistent editorial stance rather than a stray sentence. The freelancer content agrees from another angle, naming Wave among the tools that produce professional invoices quickly, and the finance buyers' guide pairs it with FreshBooks as the fastest path from time entry to a paid invoice. Read together, the record describes Wave as the default first stop rather than the tool a growing finance function graduates into.

content.title: Wave against the paid entry-level tools
content.body: Fourteen comparison records in this repository pair Wave with other products, and their pattern is unusually consistent. Wave is not recorded as the overall pick in any of the fourteen, the user-rating row goes against it every time, and the only criterion rows it takes are starting price against FreshBooks and QuickBooks. On this page it carries a rating of 4.1 out of 5 from 600 reviews. The alternatives pages tell the same story from both directions: Wave is recommended as an alternative to Expensify, Zoho Books, and Sage Intacct, and it names those same three as its own alternatives — a grouping that reads as a category match rather than a like-for-like recommendation.

content.title: Delivery, support, and what is not on file
content.body: What the material behind this page records Wave as delivered from the cloud with an API field marked available, which fits a product whose bank data and invoices are held by the service rather than on a local install. What the repository stores nowhere for Wave is a certification entry together with support-tier wording: no attestation appears alongside this product, and no record states what channels, response commitments, or paid support plans exist. Both are gaps in the dataset rather than findings about the product, so neither can be used to argue a standard is met or missed. A buyer whose approval depends on certification evidence or a support commitment should confirm those with the vendor before relying on this page.

content.title: Who Wave fits
content.body: The record points at a specific first customer: a sole trader, freelancer, or very small business sending a modest number of invoices and wanting books a bookkeeper can open without translation. The accounting-selection guide says as much by grouping Wave with entry-level tools for sole proprietors, and the ranking pages cast it as the starting point rather than the destination. The fit weakens for a business that needs inventory, project profitability, or a second legal entity, none of which our records describe for Wave, and it does not survive an evaluation that requires certification evidence, because this dataset holds none. Rated 4.1 out of 5 from 600 reviews here, it is the cheapest recorded route into a real set of books.

faqs.question: Is Wave genuinely free to use?
faqs.answer: This page records the pricing model as free with a range of Free, and the repository's pricing guide explains the shape: core accounting at no cost, with revenue drawn from payment processing fees and premium add-ons.

faqs.question: What usage limits does this repository record for Wave?
faqs.answer: A guide here recommends Wave for very basic accounting only, under five invoices and ten transactions a month, while the selection guide places it with sole proprietors whose finances are simple.

faqs.question: How does Wave collect payment from an invoice?
faqs.answer: Each invoice carries a prominent Pay Now button linking to Stripe or PayPal, and the accounting ranking records processing charges on card and bank payments in place of a subscription.

faqs.question: How does Wave fare against paid entry-level tools?
faqs.answer: Across fourteen comparison records it is never the overall pick and loses the user-rating row every time, while the starting-price row goes its way against FreshBooks and QuickBooks.

faqs.question: Who should start with Wave according to these rankings?
faqs.answer: Small teams and freelancers: six of this repository's ranking pages name Wave as the entry point for teams starting in a category, and the finance guide pairs it with FreshBooks for time-to-invoice work.

author: Emily Nakamura
learningCurve: Gentle — a working setup is reachable within the first hour
whoShouldUse: Sole proprietors, freelancers, and very small businesses sending a modest number of invoices, including teams whose first requirement is a set of books at no fixed cost that a bookkeeper can open without translation.
whoShouldNotUse: Businesses past the under-five-invoice guidance recorded in this repository's guide, teams needing inventory or project profitability, and buyers who must see certification evidence or support tiers before signing.
